questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: The history of the vacuum cleaner and cleaning at home
How to fix broken things at home instead of buying new
Why people are buying bigger houses with more storage
The popularity of getting rid of extra possessions
questions.why: Rob and Neil discuss the decluttering trend, how to do it and why.

options: The pile of clothes he leaves on the floor
A new type of wardrobe with no doors
A secret cupboard hidden under the floor
A tidy shelf for his shoes by the door
questions.why: He says he just dumps a lot of his clothes on the floor.

questions.q: What is Neil's problem with decluttering?
questions.why: He says, 'I love a good declutter - trouble is, I hate throwing things away.'

questions.q: According to Lesley Spellman, what does the Marie Kondo method start with?
questions.why: She says, 'You have to start with your clothes.'

questions.q: What do you tackle last in the Marie Kondo method?
questions.why: She says, 'And then finally you tackle sentimental things.'

questions.q: What does Rob find most difficult to get rid of?
questions.why: He says sentimental things like old letters and photos are hardest because he's sentimental.

questions.q: How did Lesley Spellman's parents' generation live?
options: They bought lots of cheap clothes
They used what they had and repaired things
questions.why: She says they came from the 'make do and mend' era after the war.

questions.q: Why does Lesley Spellman mention 'five tops for five pounds each'?
options: To recommend a good shop on the high street
To complain about the poor quality of clothes
To show how cheap goods made people buy too much
To compare today's prices with prices in the past
questions.why: She uses it to show things became affordable and consumerism went crazy.
